lead: The human eye is a compact optical sensor plus a neural processor. The cornea and lens form a focused image on the retina; rods and cones convert light into signals; the optic nerve carries them to the brain. Its response to brightness is strongly nonuniform: we notice ratios of intensity more than absolute changes, and we adapt over a huge range. This matters in image processing because a display, camera or algorithm must respect those limits when it decides what a viewer can see.
prereq: You need: 1.1 Origins and applications for what a digital image is and where processing sits.

sections.h3: The eye as an optical instrument

blocks.text: The eye is an optical instrument. Light first crosses the cornea, a clear curved layer that does most of the bending. It then passes through the aqueous humour, a watery fluid, and through the pupil. The iris is the colored ring that opens or closes the pupil; the pupil is the aperture that controls how much light enters. The lens sits behind the pupil. It is flexible and changes shape to focus on near or far objects. This change is called accommodation. The vitreous humour, a jelly-like fluid, fills the space behind the lens and holds the retina in place. The cornea and lens together form an inverted, reduced image on the retina. The retina is the sensor surface: it contains light-sensitive cells. Pupil control is fast, like a camera aperture; accommodation is slower, like autofocus. A camera can imitate both, but the eye does not produce a uniform pixel grid. Its sampling and sensitivity vary across the retina. Some syllabi call this set of ideas elements of visual perception.

sections.h3: Retina: rods, cones, fovea and blind spot

blocks.text: The retina has two main types of photoreceptor. Rods work in dim light. They are many, they are sensitive, and they do not signal color. Cones work in brighter light. They signal color and fine detail. The fovea is a small central pit packed with cones. When you look directly at a word, its image falls on the fovea. Away from the fovea, rods dominate and acuity falls. This is why you move your eyes to read. The optic nerve leaves the retina at a point with no photoreceptors, the blind spot. The brain fills in the missing area, so you do not see a hole. The retina also performs early processing before signals leave the eye. Its cells compare neighboring responses, sharpen edges and compress the range of light levels. So vision is not a camera sending raw pixels. The eye sends a processed signal. For image processing, the lesson is that spatial resolution and brightness sensitivity are not uniform over the field of view. A fixed grid of pixels is a useful engineering model, not a copy of the retina. Color behavior is covered in 1.9 Color models.

Brightness adaptation is the eye's change of sensitivity with light level. In dark adaptation, the pupil widens and the photoreceptors become more sensitive over minutes. In light adaptation, the reverse happens quickly. This lets you read a phone at night and then step into sunlight, though not instantly. Brightness discrimination is the ability to detect a small change in intensity. The smallest detectable change is the just noticeable difference, written ΔI. The background intensity is I. Over a middle range, the ratio ΔI/I is roughly constant. This ratio is the Weber ratio, and the constant is the Weber fraction k. A small k means fine discrimination. If I doubles, the smallest detectable ΔI also roughly doubles. A fixed ΔI is therefore not equally visible at all levels. The exact k varies with background, observer and measurement. Contrast sensitivity describes how well the eye sees patterns of different spatial frequency at low contrast. It is high for some middle frequencies and falls for very fine or very coarse patterns. Mach bands are bright and dark bands seen near an edge. They appear because neighboring retinal responses inhibit each other. The eye does not report intensity directly; it reports local contrast. A display with limited gray levels, or an algorithm that stretches contrast, must respect these limits. Otherwise smooth gradients can show false bands.

blocks.where: ΔI is the smallest detectable change in intensity; I is the background intensity; k is the Weber fraction, a dimensionless number roughly constant over a middle range.

examples.question: A display has background intensity I = 50 cd/m². A test patch is just noticeable when its intensity is 52 cd/m². Find ΔI and the approximate Weber fraction. If the background rises to 100 cd/m² at the same fraction, estimate the new just-noticeable ΔI.
steps: Identify the background intensity I = 50 cd/m² and the just-noticeable test intensity I + ΔI = 52 cd/m².
Find the intensity change: ΔI = 52 − 50 = 2 cd/m².
Find the Weber fraction: ΔI/I = 2/50 = 0.04. This is dimensionless.
At I = 100 cd/m², use the same fraction: ΔI ≈ 0.04 × 100 = 4 cd/m².
examples.answer: ΔI = 2 cd/m², ΔI/I = 0.04, and at I = 100 cd/m² the new just-noticeable ΔI is about 4 cd/m².
examples.check:
I = 50.0
I_test = 52.0
delta_I = I_test - I
ratio = delta_I / I
I_new = 100.0
delta_I_new = ratio * I_new
print(delta_I)
print(ratio)
print(delta_I_new)

traps: Pupil and lens are not the same control. The pupil changes aperture and light level; the lens changes focus by accommodation.
Rods and cones are not interchangeable. Rods give dim-light vision without color; cones give color and detail in brighter light.
The Weber ratio is ΔI/I, not ΔI. At a higher background I, the same ratio allows a larger absolute change ΔI.
The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the retina. It is not the fovea, and it is not a lack of attention.
Fovea does not mean high light sensitivity. It means high acuity from dense cones; rods dominate in dim peripheral vision.

quiz.q: Which part of the eye controls the amount of light entering?
quiz.a: The iris controls the pupil. The pupil is the opening that acts as the aperture.

quiz.q: Why does the fovea give sharp vision?
quiz.a: The fovea has a high density of cones and little convergence, so detail is sampled finely. It needs good light.

quiz.q: A background has I = 80 cd/m². The Weber fraction is 0.05. Find the smallest detectable ΔI and the just-noticeable test intensity.
A 1 cd/m² step is visible on a dark screen but not on a bright screen. Explain using the Weber ratio.
quiz.a: On a bright screen I is large, so ΔI/I is small; the relative change is below threshold. On a dark screen I is small, so the same ΔI is a larger fraction and becomes visible.

quiz.q: How is contrast sensitivity different from brightness discrimination?
quiz.a: Brightness discrimination is detection of an intensity change on a background. Contrast sensitivity is detection of a pattern at low contrast across spatial frequencies. They are related but not identical.

quiz.q: At I = 60 cd/m², ΔI = 3 cd/m² is just noticeable. Estimate ΔI at I = 150 cd/m² with the same Weber fraction.
Why can a smooth gradient on an 8-bit display show false bands, and how do eye properties matter?
quiz.a: An 8-bit display has only 256 intensity levels. In some regions the step between levels exceeds ΔI, so just-noticeable steps appear. The eye is sensitive to ratios, so bands are more visible at low intensities and in smooth areas. Dithering or more levels reduces them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Eye-inspired models appear in tone mapping for high dynamic range photos, in perceptual image quality metrics, and in display design for phones and AR glasses. Researchers study retinal processing to build event cameras and low-power vision sensors that report changes rather than full frames. Search for human visual system, Weber law, contrast sensitivity function, Mach bands, and retinal ganglion cell receptive fields. These ideas return when you judge whether an enhancement result looks natural.
